actions.reason:
I measured two variants of the train update path and both were byte-identical to the parent. Neither reached the 1% minimum, so there is nothing to submit.

1. RegexTokenizer.train now gets each new pair's count by summing its occurrence list in C (sum(map(counts_at, where[p]))). This drops one Python dict update per new-pair occurrence in the merge loop. train_ir ratio was 0.9975 (325085510 -> 324278255).
2. On top of that, I built the pair index with a defaultdict append and moved BasicTokenizer's neighbour counting into Counter(map(itemgetter, filter(...))). train_ir ratio was 0.9977, so the extra edits added nothing. The per-call Python overhead of Counter probably cancels what the C-level counting saves on parts lists this short.

The library's share of train_ir now looks small next to the fixed cost of interpreter startup, importing regex and compiling the pattern. Small edits to the merge loop save under 1M instructions, against the roughly 3.3M needed. Reaching the bar would likely take a structural change to RegexTokenizer.train, not more small edits.

journal.text:
I changed the train update path in minbpe/regex.py. In RegexTokenizer.train, each new pair's count now comes from summing its occurrence list in C, sum(map(counts_at, where[p])). This removes one Python dict update per new-pair occurrence in the merge loop. A second variant also cut the merge helper in minbpe/basic.py from 18 lines to 7 and tidied regex.py imports.

Both variants gave identical outputs to the parent. Evaluation 1 moved train_ir from 325085510 to 324278255, ratio 0.9975, with encode_ir at 1.0000. Evaluation 3 gave train_ir 0.9977 and encode_ir 0.9995. Both were rejected because the required ratio is 0.9900. Neither change helped enough, and I submitted nothing.

The dict updates in the merge loop are not where train spends its instructions. Removing them saves about a quarter of a percent.

Next I should profile train before editing and find the dominant cost. That may be the per-chunk regex split or the pair counting over all chunks on every merge.
